A hollow in the old ash by the stream. I have it to myself. The bark is thick, the entrance is narrow. I keep the owlets safe inside. The stream runs through the hollow.

My home is the hollow of the old oak in the hollow of the wood. It is a round hole, just big enough for me to fit in. The bark is rough and cold, but I have a lining of moss and leaves. I sit on a dry branch inside, and I can hear the wood all around me. It is quiet there, and it is mine.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark flaky. I sit in the hollow with my mate. She is on the other side of the hollow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "e-wee".
A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the road. The oak is in the meadow near the stream. The hollow is dry, and the bark is rough. I sit in it and call at dusk.

My home is the hollow of the old oak, three trees from the stream. It is round, wide enough for me to turn in, and deep enough for me to sleep through the night. The wood is soft and warm, and I have a small nest of moss and leaves inside. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. It is quiet, but not too quiet. I am safe here, and I keep it clean.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old, its bark cracked and rough, and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head. I line it with dry leaves and feathers. The wind comes through the cracks in winter.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I can see the meadow from it, the lane, the stream, the lane, the house, the lane. The hollow is dark, cold, and dry in winter. I line it with dry leaves and a bit of wool.
A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the road. It is dark and damp, and I line it with moss and feathers. The floor is soft, and I sleep in it.

A hollow in an old oak, three branches down from the top, where the wind does not go. I have been there for three winters. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the lane comes in. I sit in the hollow with my head out, listening for the lane.

My home is a hollow in an old oak. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit in the hollow, and the wind comes through the cracks. I can hear the stream below and the road that runs past the meadow. The hollow is safe, and I am safe here. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the hollow, and the chee-chee answers from the wood.
A hollow in an old oak. I can see the oak from my perch on the fence post by the lane. It is dark and dry inside, with a soft lining of dry leaves. The owlet is warm in the nest.

A hollow in an old oak, in a hollow of a large ash. I have this hollow for three winters now. It is dark and damp, and the wind comes through the cracks. I line it with leaves and down from the underbelly of mice.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and dry inside, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to fit through. A hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. It is round, about the size of a man's head, and I line it with dry leaves and down from my own feathers. It faces east, so the first light touches it.
A hollow in the ash by the stream. It is wide enough for me to turn my head and see through, and deep enough for the storm to keep out. I have a roost in the ivy at the top of the ash.
A hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. The tree is hollow inside, wide enough for me to sit up and turn my head. The bark is rough and cold. I sit on the floor of the hollow and call from there.
